# Paper Selected
Bias in error estimation when using cross-validation for model selection by Varma and Simon (2006)

# Paper Summary

## Key Ideas

In datasets with a small number of samples, cross-validation (CV) is often used to estimate the error of a model, and thus help with model selection. CV has been shown to be unbiased if all aspects of model training are done inside the CV loop, including feature selection, classifier type selection, and classifier parameter tuning. However, if this process is violated, it leads to biased error estimates. This is especially true for datasets with a small number of samples and a large number of features, which is common in microarray data.

The paper used 1000 "null" simulated datasets consisting of 40 samples and 6000 features for classifier training using both shrunken centroids and support vector machine (SVM) classifiers. The null datasets included a 50/50 split of Class 1 and Class 2. The authors found that when feature selection and classifier parameter tuning to minimize errors were done outside of the CV loop, CV can produce biased models. Although 10-fold CV and leave-one-out CV (LOOCV) resampling methods were evaluated in this study, the result was shown to be present in all CV methods.

The authors also presented a nested CV method that was used to develop a more unbiased model. This method was evaluated using the same simulated datasets and used both shrunken centroids and SVM classifiers. In the nested CV method, the outer CV loop used a LOOCV approach, while the inner CV loop used a 10-fold CV approach to determine the classifier parameters and model. Once the inner CV loop was completed, the model was evaluated on the left out sample from the outer CV loop. The average error from the outer CV loop was shown to be effective in reducing model bias over the simulated datasets.

STOP DOING: Standard CV with datasets that include a small number of samples and a large number of features.

START DOING: Nested CV with similarly sized datasets.

## Example Demonstrating the Key Ideas

The authors developed classifiers on the simulated null datasets using both shrunken centroids and SVM classifiers. The shrunken centroids and SVM classifiers resulted in less than 30% training error 18.5% and 22.2% of the time, respectively. The mean bias for the models was found to be -12.2% and -8.3%, respectively. The nested CV method was found to have only a slight overestimate of the true error, witha mean bias of 4.2%.

## Other Things I Learned

A classifier is a model for categorical data.

The shrunken centroids classifier works by shrinking the centroids of each class towards the overall data centroid using the within class standard deviation.

The support vector machine (SVM) classifier works by finding a hyperplane that separates the classes by a maximum margin. 

Kernels are the representation of scalar products in a transformed feature space.

Leave-One-Out-CV (LOOCV) is a form of CV in which one sample is left out during each CV fold. Error is then computed on the left out sample. This is done for datasets with very small sample sizes.


# Simulation Ideas

It would be interesting to recreate this simulation to learn more about shrunken centroids and SVM classifiers and to help better understand the bias in error estimation when using CV for model selection. It would also be interesting to do a parametric study on datasets with a different number of samples and features to see how the bias changes as the dataset dimensions change.
